pr.title: gvn: avoid creating overlapping assignments
pr.description:
Quick fix #141038, as I couldn't find a way to avoid in-place modification. I'm considering handling all `rvalue` modifications within the `visit_statement` function.

r? mir-opt
pr.author: dianqk

issues.title: GVN misunderstands aliasing, can create overlapping assignments

processing.reason: The PR's incorrect transformation is the GVN rewrite `(*dst) = Adt::Some(copy field)` -> `(*dst) = copy (*src)` where the dereferenced LHS and the copied source place may alias. The regression test is a MIR-shape test (`//@ test-mir-pass: GVN`) and does not assert a runtime value. In the issue, the only observable failure of the rewritten program is UB: Miri reports ``copy_nonoverlapping` called on overlapping ranges`` at the transformed assignment. Consequently, any input that actually exhibits the aliasing (source overlapping destination) makes the transformed function fail Miri, while any non-overlapping input makes the original aggregate write and the copy write value-equivalent (assuming the same source/destination state). There is therefore no source-grounded concrete input for which both original and transformed executions are defined under Miri and produce different numeric/boolean/character results. Producing a value difference would require adding a separate hidden-mutation/stale-value scenario (e.g. mutating the source through a local GVN does not invalidate) or replacing the overlapping MIR copy with a read-then-write lowering that suppresses the very UB this PR fixes; both would encode a different transformation rather than the historical overlapping-assignment bug. Hence no valid pair can be validated under the required constraints.

analysis.originalLogic: GVN's aggregate simplification attempted to replace an aggregate assignment with a copy from an existing place when the source could be represented as a place and its type matched the aggregate type. In `simplify_aggregate_to_copy`, it called `try_as_place(copy_from_local_value, location, true)`, compared `rvalue.ty(...)` with `place.ty(...).ty`, then unconditionally inserted `place.local` into `reused_locals`, rewrote the rvalue to `Rvalue::Use(Operand::Copy(place))`, and returned `Some(copy_from_local_value)`. The original code did not receive the assignment LHS, so it could perform this rewrite even when the LHS was a dereference/projection rather than a local.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation replaced an aggregate RHS such as `(*_2) = Adt::Some(copy _3)` with `(*_2) = copy (*_4)` when `_4` aliases the destination through `_2`. This creates an assignment whose source and destination overlap. The issue describes the result as: "`copy_nonoverlapping` called on overlapping ranges", and the patch says to "Avoid creating `*a = copy (*b)`, as they might be aliases resulting in overlapping assignments." The fix passes the LHS into `simplify_rvalue`/`simplify_aggregate`/`simplify_aggregate_to_copy` and only rewrites to `Rvalue::Use(Operand::Copy(place))` when `lhs.as_local().is_some()`. If the LHS is not local, it still returns the value index but leaves the aggregate rvalue unchanged.
analysis.inputDomain: GVN input MIR where a statement assigns an aggregate to a non-local/dereferenced place, and the aggregate's field value can be represented by a place reachable through a pointer/reference that aliases the assignment destination. The source and aggregate type must match so `simplify_aggregate_to_copy` is eligible. A minimal pair can use the regression shape: `_33 = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(_17); _73 = &(*_33); _48 = Field(Variant((*_73), 1), 0);` followed by either the correct `(*_33) = Adt::Some(_48);` or the wrong transformed `(*_33) = copy(*_73);` (the issue's MIR diff shows `(*_2) = Adt::Some(copy _3);` becoming `(*_2) = copy (*_4);`). Both programs differ only in that final RHS rewrite.
analysis.summary: Confirmed GVN bug fix: aggregate-to-copy simplification could rewrite an aggregate assignment whose LHS is a dereference into `*a = copy (*b)` even when `a` and `b` alias, producing an overlapping assignment. GVN now only performs this rewrite when the LHS is a local; otherwise it leaves the aggregate assignment intact.
analysis.trigger: GVN simplifies an aggregate assignment to copy from an existing place, and the assignment LHS is not a local but a projection/dereference whose referent may alias the copied place.
preconditions: GVN is processing an assignment whose RHS is an aggregate.
`try_as_place(copy_from_local_value, location, true)` finds an eligible source place.
The aggregate type equals the source place's type.
The assignment LHS is projected (for example `(*_2)`) rather than a local, so the old code could create an aliasing copy assignment.
pitfalls: Do not rewrite an aggregate assignment to a plain copy solely because the types match; aliasing between the projected LHS and copied place must be considered.
The historical fix uses `lhs.as_local().is_some()` as a broad guard, so it also avoids non-deref projections; the FIXME notes allowed projections could be added later.
Returning `Some(copy_from_local_value)` after declining the rewrite is not evidence that the rvalue was rewritten; the rvalue must remain the aggregate.
Do not conflate this alias/overlap issue with separate conditions such as borrowing restrictions or post-copy overwrites.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a focused `tests/mir-opt` regression using `//@ test-mir-pass: GVN` and `custom_mir`. Construct the aliasing raw-pointer/reference pattern, then check the post-GVN assignment remains `(*[[PTR]]) = Adt::Some(copy {{.*}});` rather than becoming `(*[[PTR]]) = copy (*[[REF]]);`. Use `// EMIT_MIR gvn_overlapping.overlapping.GVN.diff` and inspect the before/after diff to ensure the aggregate assignment is unchanged by GVN. The added test includes the comment `// Check that we do not create overlapping assignments.`
evidence: GVN misunderstands aliasing, can create overlapping assignments
Avoid creating `*a = copy (*b)`, as they might be aliases resulting in overlapping assignments.
Check that we do not create overlapping assignments.
